parsing_res_list.block_content: Tension membrane response can develop in reinforced masonry walls at large deflections if there is: 1) fully developed reinforcing bars throughout the span and into the supports; and 2) supports with adequate in-plane rigidity for one-way responding walls. The bars will not remain fully developed throughout the span if composite action between the grout and reinforcing steel deteriorates at high steel strains. Sufficient testing has not been performed to develop specific design and detailing requirements for masonry walls to provide tension membrane resistance during response to blast loads. Also, boundary conditions that allow tension membrane response are not typical in reinforced masonry wall construction. Thus, membrane action may develop in reinforced masonry walls with adequate supports and reinforcing details, but design approaches verified with blast test data are not available.
In summary, tension and compression membrane action should not typically be considered in the design or analysis of masonry walls for explosives safety applications.

The principles for dynamic analysis of structural components subject to blast loads presented in Chapter 3 of this document apply to blast analyses of masonry walls.Therefore, the dynamic response of masonry walls can be modeled using an equivalent SDOF system. The SDOF system consists of a mass-spring system with a mass that is defined by the wall mass and a load-mass factor, and a spring that is defined by a resistance-deflection relationship representing the response of the wall to the blast load (i.e. typically a uniform pressure loading). The wall mass is calculated based on the wall weight and the load-mass factor is determined based on the wall boundary conditions and associated deflected shape of the wall from blast load as discussed in Section 3-7.

The resistance-deflection relationship for flexural response is described in Chapter 3.This approach should be used to determine the resistance-deflection relationship for masonry walls. The ultimate dynamic moment capacity and moment of inertia for the wall should be determined as discussed in Sections 6.8 and 6.9 for reinforced and unreinforced masonry walls, respectively. At deflections greater than the yield deflection causing the ultimate flexural resistance, the response of reinforced masonry walls may be considered ductile (i.e. constant resistance equal to the ultimate flexural resistance with increasing deflection), while the response of unreinforced masonry walls is considered britle and the flexural resistance goes to zero. Unreinforced masonry walls develop additional resistance at deflections greater than the yield deflection from the effects of in-plane axial force, including self-weight, which cause arching response described in Section 6-9. Tension membrane response can develop in reinforced masonry walls at large
deflections if there is: 1) fully developed reinforcing bars throughout the span and into
the supports; and 2) supports with adequate in-plane rigidity for one-way responding
walls. The bars will not remain fully developed throughout the span if composite action
between the grout and reinforcing steel deteriorates at high steel strains. Sufficient
testing has not been performed to develop specific design and detailing requirements
for masonry walls to provide tension membrane resistance during response to blast
loads. Also, boundary conditions that allow tension membrane response are not typical
in reinforced masonry wall construction. Thus, membrane action may develop in
reinforced masonry walls with adequate supports and reinforcing details, but design
approaches verified with blast test data are not available.
In summary, tension and compression membrane action should not typically be
considered in the design or analysis of masonry walls for explosives safety applications.

defined by the wall mass and a load-mass factor, and a spring that is defined by a
resistance-deflection relationship representing the response of the wall to the blast load
(i.e. typically a uniform pressure loading). The wall mass is calculated based on the wall
weight and the load-mass factor is determined based on the wall boundary conditions
and associated deflected shape of the wall from blast load as discussed in Section 3-7.
